article_title: It's About Time
citation: BetsAnn Smith. (1998). It's About Time: Opportunities to Learn in Chicago's Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: Nest a full 300-minute instructional program within a school day of 360-400 minutes
description: The report argues that instructional time policy must build in realistic room for the human and operational demands of elementary classrooms rather than a maximally compressed schedule. Its observations showed schools operating "a highly compressed schedule" in which non-instructional demands spill into officially allotted instruction time. It concludes that a 300-minutes-a-day instructional program must be nested within a school day of 360-400 minutes, depending on lunch organization and whether recess is restored.
requirements: School day length must be extended beyond the current 330-minute closed campus schedule to absorb operational demands without eroding instruction.
constraints: The report notes Chicago's largely disadvantaged schools are asked to make achievement gains in less time than more advantaged surrounding systems; new charter schools chose 60-90 minutes longer days.
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools elementary students
target_learning_goals: Increasing delivered instructional time across the full academic program
examples: The report observes that most new Chicago charter schools chose to operate 60 to 90 minutes longer each day than the standard CPS school day.
key_sources: BetsAnn Smith. (1998). It's About Time: Opportunities to Learn in Chicago's Elementary Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/its-about-time-opportunities-learn

article_title: Preparing Teachers For Deeper Learning
citation: Karen Cator, Carri Schneider, Tom Vander Ark. (2014). Preparing Teachers for Deeper Learning: Competency-Based Teacher Preparation and Development. Digital Promise / Getting Smart. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Next-generation teacher preparation and PD should offer teacher control over time, place, path and/or pace, balanced goals, job-embedded integration, and competency-based progression
description: The paper's central design recommendation is that high-quality teacher preparation and ongoing professional learning should mirror the personalized learning advocated for students. Its stated principles are "some element of teacher control over time, place, path and/or pace;" balance between teacher-defined, administrative, and school/district goals; "job-embedded and meaningful integration into classroom practice;" and competency-based progression. The paper argues these same principles applied to students' blended learning can and should be applied to teacher learning.
requirements: Blended structures that combine online learning with onsite experiences
Adult learning conditions of adaptability, productivity and value given teachers' time and money constraints
constraints: The paper frames these as design principles for a envisioned system rather than tested interventions
target_learners: Pre-service teachers
Practicing K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Teaching competencies for personalized, blended Deeper Learning environments
Continuous development of teacher competency throughout their careers
examples: Western Governors University offers self-paced, competency-based teacher preparation in which student teachers can test out of subjects; Summit Public Schools gives teachers two-week self-directed PD chunks four times a year
key_sources: Karen Cator, Carri Schneider, Tom Vander Ark. (2014). Preparing Teachers for Deeper Learning: Competency-Based Teacher Preparation and Development. Digital Promise / Getting Smart. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/a1928fce-2d47-429b-8e81-fbeb9ce079c3

article_title: Combining academic, noncognitive, and college knowledge measures to identify students not on track for college: A data-driven approach
citation: James Soland. (2017). Combining Academic, Noncognitive, and College Knowledge Measures to Identify Students Not on Track For College: A Data-Driven Approach. Research & Practice in Assessment, Volume Twelve, Summer 2017. https://rpajournal.com
title: National Education Longitudinal Survey (NELS) dataset
description: NELS is a nationally representative longitudinal dataset tracking students from their 8th-grade year in 1988 through 2000, including recorded postsecondary outcomes and thousands of student survey items. Baseline data were collected on 12,144 students, of whom 9,601 (79 percent) attended college and roughly 8,800 persisted for a semester. The author chose NELS over the more recent ELS because it includes a broader range of student survey items, and used 8th- and 10th-grade measures to predict college readiness.
requirements: Missing predictor values require nominal missing categories or fully conditional imputation, which the article applies
constraints: NELS survey items are not organized by construct
Not all constructs of interest are included; it largely predates grit and growth-mindset measures
target_learners: 8th- and 10th-grade students followed into postsecondary education
target_learning_goals: Predicting college enrollment and persistence to inform readiness supports
examples: Themes in the survey items include postsecondary aspirations and expectations, home environment, self-esteem and locus of control, and college choice factors

article_title: Understanding the At-Risk Indicator: Nevada's Pupil-Centered Funding Plan
citation: Tanner, S., Krausen, K., Garcia, B., & Brown, A. (2025). Understanding the At-risk indicator: Nevada's Pupil-Centered Funding Plan. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Nevada's GRAD score: a machine learning–generated At-risk indicator in a school funding formula
description: The GRAD score is a machine learning output produced within Nevada's Infinite Campus system, described as the first such indicator used in a state funding formula. The report states that "The GRAD score is calculated by a machine learning program from Infinite Campus that analyzes approximately 70 data points about a student in areas including academic performance, attendance, behavior, home, and economic stability." Students in the lowest quintile of GRAD scores are designated At-risk and generate a 0.35 weight above the Statewide Base for their schools, subject to unduplicated counting rules.
requirements: Student data across academic performance, attendance, behavior, home, and economic stability must flow into the Infinite Campus system so the algorithm can score each student
A statewide lowest-quintile cutoff must be computed annually (on or around October 1) to convert scores into At-risk designations
constraints: Students who also qualify for special education or English Learner status are funded in those categories, not as At-risk, due to unduplicated counts
Funding counts come from the prior fiscal year's October 1 validation data, so budgets rely on year-old identifications
target_learners: K-12 public school students in Nevada scoring in the lowest quintile of GRAD scores
target_learning_goals: Identifying students at risk of not graduating with their cohort so additional funding reaches their schools
examples: In fiscal year 2025 the Statewide Base was $9,414 per student, so each At-risk student generated an additional $3,294 for their LEA
key_sources: Tanner, S., Krausen, K., Garcia, B., & Brown, A. (2025). Understanding the At-risk indicator: Nevada's Pupil-Centered Funding Plan. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677573

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Three-type taxonomy of newcomer schools: programs-within-a-school, transitional, and comprehensive
description: The report organizes newcomer schools into three structural types. "These newcomer schools use a standalone facility" distinguishes transitional and comprehensive schools, while programs-within-a-school are "embedded programs co-located at a traditional school" where newcomers join recess, meals, electives, and sports with host-school students. The types differ in enrollment duration and exit pathways: transitional schools are designed for 1-2 years, while comprehensive schools let students remain through graduation.

constraints: Characteristics vary by district vision, economic resources, teacher talent, approach to supporting English Learners, facilities, and newcomer numbers and circumstances
target_learners: Recently-arrived K-12 immigrant, refugee, and asylee students not proficient in English
target_learning_goals: English language acquisition
acculturation to American schools
core content remediation and grade-level instruction
examples: Lewiston High School and Winooski are programs-within-a-school; Newcomer Academy and Rochester International Academy are transitional; The Manhattan International High School is comprehensive

title: Newcomer schools as self-contained learning environments for recently-arrived immigrant English Learners

specialized supports addressing academic, social, and emotional needs

learning-to-learn skills
grade-level content mastery

grade-level content mastery
successful transition to traditional schools or college

article_title: Priced out: How the Wrong Financial-Aid Policies Hurt Low-Income Students
citation: Mamie Lynch, Jennifer Engle, and José L. Cruz. (2011). Priced Out: How the Wrong Financial-Aid Policies Hurt Low-Income Students. The Education Trust. https://www.collegeresults.org
title: Evaluate financial-aid policies by whether they primarily benefit low-income students, remove access barriers, and provide awards large enough to influence choices and success
description: The report proposes that policymakers apply a set of screening questions to any financial-aid policy at the federal, state, or institutional level. The questions ask whether the policy "primarily benefit[s] low-income students," whether low-income students can "fully tap financial assistance" without technical barriers, and whether awards are "large enough to influence the choices—and success rates—of low-income students." The report grounds this in its finding that current aid choices increasingly steer funds toward affluent students.
requirements: Policymakers at federal, state, and institutional levels must apply the criteria when setting financial-aid policy
constraints: The report notes net-price data cannot show how institutions allocate aid across income brackets, only what low-income students pay after all grant aid
target_learners: low-income undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: college access and affordability
postsecondary attainment
examples: The report's executive summary and conclusion both print the three-question test for decision makers setting financial-aid policy

article_title: Next Generation Accountability: A Vision for School Improvement under ESSA
citation: Adams, C. M., Ford, T. G., Forsyth, P. B., Ware, J. K., Olsen, J. J., Lepine, J. A., Sr., Barnes, L. B., Khojasteh, J., & Mwavita, M. (2017). Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability
title: Next generation accountability framework: shared accountability, adaptive improvement, and informational significance in a two-stage design
description: The report advances a framework for school accountability under ESSA governed by three principles: shared accountability, in which "performance responsibility is distributed across the system's components"; adaptive improvement, acknowledging that school capacities differ greatly; and informational significance, replacing a single composite with a broad palette of functionally significant indicators. It features a two-stage design: Stage One is formative, providing schools useful information for their own improvement decisions; Stage Two is aggressive, identifying and transforming schools in catastrophic failure. Schools are viewed as systems whose outcomes result from the quality of their resources and processes.

constraints: Stage Two applies to schools in catastrophic failure; Stage One is more formative than summative

college and career readiness
examples: The framework is operationalized in the Educational Quality and Improvement Profile (EQuIP) with resource, process, and outcome indicators

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: Give students newly designed datasets to investigate with AI rather than widely used public datasets with published worked analyses
description: Because widely used public datasets carry tutorials and worked analyses that models may have encountered during training, students may receive explanations drawn from existing analyses without practicing how to investigate unfamiliar data in collaboration with AI. The article argues teaching cases should feature "newly designed relationships that students must examine using the supplied data," with deliberately designed patterns and verified reference answers so instructors can assess discoveries and reasoning. In AI-assisted classes, assessment can consider the questions students ask, the comparisons they choose, and how they justify their conclusions.

constraints: A new case still contains familiar business concepts and analytical methods an AI model can use; students must establish which explanations fit their particular dataset
target_learners: undergraduate business analytics students working with AI assistants
target_learning_goals: investigating unfamiliar data
directing and evaluating AI assistance
checking supporting evidence
examples: WindowDash asks students to report at least five findings from a case with nine intended patterns, while the pattern inventory and reference solution remain with the instructor

article_title: Generative AI as a Didactic-Pedagogical Mediator: Rethinking Human Roles and Pedagogical Design in Higher Education
citation: Moganadas SR, Marín-González F, Nun SH and Gan CL (2026) Generative AI as a didactic-pedagogical mediator: rethinking human roles and pedagogical design in higher education. Front. Educ. 11:1856839. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1856839
title: Nested instructor-student-GenAI triadic conceptual model for higher education
description: The article proposes a triadic model that replaces the traditional instructor-student dyad with an interdependent relationship among instructors, students, GenAI outputs, and institutional conditions. It positions GenAI as "a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator operating within a shared didactic mediation space." The model spans three interdependent levels: micro (course-and-lesson-level interactions), meso (institutional governance arrangements), and macro (stakeholder and infrastructural ecosystem). Knowledge construction emerges through students' active meaning-making among human participants, AI outputs, disciplinary criteria, and institutional expectations.

constraints: The model specifies proposed relationships rather than a fixed sequence of interaction or causal effects
It is a conceptual model derived from synthesis, not yet empirically validated
target_learners: higher education students, including novice learners new to HE, a subject, or GenAI use
target_learning_goals: learner agency
AI literacy
disciplinary knowledge construction
ethical judgment
examples: The article illustrates the model with a writing-task scenario in which GenAI generates an outline or formative feedback while the instructor specifies appropriate AI use, disclosure, and assessment criteria

citation: Habibullah, A., Alshoibi, Y., Alshiekh, M., Khan, S., & Khan, N. (2026). Where LLM graders succeed and break: Evidence from two computer-science exams. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29333
title: Never instruct an LLM grader to withhold credit, and verify the grader against the prompt and the exam before deployment
description: The article's deployment guidance is to avoid credit-withholding instructions in grader prompts, because both policy sentences collapse graders on their own, unordered by parameter count, and under-grading harms students who attempted the work in good faith. It further advises verifying the model against the prompt and the exam, evaluating several prompt variants including instructor-written ones, and reporting bias alongside MAE so the direction of harm is visible.

Bias reported alongside MAE
constraints: On exams where models over-mark at neutral, the same preamble can improve MAE by cancelling bias, so its effect must be checked per exam

target_learning_goals: Accurate, rubric-aligned automated grading of student work
examples: The strict preset's S2 sentence alone stopped Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-Small-24B grading; Flash-Lite's lenient and strict runs had comparable MAE with opposite-signed bias (+4.01 vs. −5.44)

citation: Julián Méndez, Lukas Gerlach, Tobias Wieland, Alex Ivliev, Markus Krötzsch, Raimund Dachselt. (2026). Evaluating a Visual Query Tracer and Builder for Learning Declarative Logic Programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18864
title: Nemo Explain Visualizer (nev): an interactive visual query tracer and builder for Datalog reasoning
description: Nemo Explain Visualizer (nev) is a free, open-source web-based visual explanation tool for the Nemo Datalog reasoner, described as "an interactive visual query tracer and builder for Nemo". Its interface combines a main visual trace editor, an indented tree explorer view, and a fact-tables view. It supports type 1 queries (proof traces for individual facts) and type 2 queries that take a proof-tree shape and populate it with facts, letting users add or remove rules, restrict queries, focus on a rule, and undo/redo modifications.

constraints: The article states the tool is without specific learning features; it was designed with and for expert users for debugging and development

expert Datalog developers
target_learning_goals: understanding rule-based reasoning and proof traces in Datalog
debugging and inspecting Datalog programs
examples: In the study, participants used nev to inspect traces, find minimal-cost paths, and modify queries to find paths of specific length on weighted graphs

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Neo-ecological restructuring of connectedness: virtual microsystems and AI as a quasi-people actor
description: Drawing on Navarro and Tudge's neo-ecological theory, the article describes how microsystems split into parallel physical and virtual categories, with technology treated as 'an actor capable of generating proximal developmental processes' rather than a mere tool. The updated theory formally recognizes anthropomorphic AI as a quasi-people actor within virtual microsystems. Because AI is neither a real human nor a passive tool but can sustain long-term personalized two-way interaction, its entry into adolescents' daily ecologies creates the theoretical necessity of defining artificial intelligence connectedness as an independent subtype of connectedness.
requirements: The framework maintains continuity with Bronfenbrenner's PPCT model, extending only the microsystem structure.
constraints: The article notes competing frameworks such as Ecological Techno-Microsystem Theory treat technology only as an influencing factor within the microsystem, not an independent ecological level.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: developmental analysis of digital-era social ecologies
examples: Virtual microsystem interactions are shaped by platform structures and affordances such as synchronicity, anonymity, information retention, and algorithmic recommendation.

citation: Xie, X., Zhang, L. J., & Wilson, A. J. (2025). Comparing ChatGPT Feedback and Peer Feedback in Shaping Students' Evaluative Judgement of Statistical Analysis: A Case Study. Behavioral Sciences, 15(7), 884. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs15070884
title: Nelson's tripartite framework of evaluative judgement (hard, soft, dynamic) adapted to statistical data analysis
description: The study adopts Nelson's (2018) tripartite framework, in which "Nelson distinguishes between three interrelated dimensions of evaluative judgement: hard, soft, and dynamic." Hard judgement is the "critical, accuracy-oriented appraisal of statistical outputs"; soft judgement assesses the value, relevance and significance of findings; dynamic judgement monitors the whole analytical process as iterative. The article redefines all three dimensions for statistical contexts and uses them as the deductive coding template for its thematic analysis.

Critical assessment of statistical methods and outputs

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Negative knowledge: experientially acquired knowledge about what is wrong and to be avoided
description: The article defines negative knowledge as "experientially acquired knowledge about what is wrong and what is to be avoided during performance in a given work situation". Grounded in constructivist theorization, knowledge is a "map of what reality allows us to do", and negative knowledge is "non-viable knowledge that is heuristically valuable" — knowing what is wrong helps identify viable paths. constraints: The article works from an individual, cognitive perspective before expanding to a socio-cultural level

learning from errors
expertise development

article_title: Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults
citation: J. A. Anguera, J. Boccanfuso, J. L. Rintoul, O. Al-Hashimi, F. Faraji, J. Janowich, E. Kong, Y. Larraburo, C. Rolle, E. Johnston & A. Gazzaley. (2013). Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults. Nature 501. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12486
title: NeuroRacer: a custom-designed three-dimensional video game for assessing and training multitasking-based cognitive control
description: NeuroRacer is a custom-designed three-dimensional video game combining a perceptual discrimination 'sign task' with a concurrent visuomotor 'driving task', used both diagnostically (measuring d' multitasking cost) and as a training platform. The article describes it as a tool that "can be used to assess cognitive abilities across the lifespan, evaluate underlying neural mechanisms, and serve as a powerful tool for cognitive enhancement". Training used an adaptive staircase algorithm adjusting each component task after each 3-min run, with rewards given only when both tasks improved beyond 80%.

Home training on a laptop with compliance monitoring (scheduled sessions, wireless data transfer, weekly contact)

Training benefits on untrained tasks were specific to working memory and sustained attention, with no group × session interactions on processing speed tasks

adults across the lifespan aged 20–79 (assessment)

sustained attention
working memory

A diagnostic version was played by 174 participants spanning six decades to measure multitasking cost

citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Dede's neomillennial learning styles framework
description: Dede (2005) presented a framework of "neomillennial learning styles" based on new digital literacies, describing the learning strengths and preferences technology-using people bring to educational settings. The framework includes fluency in multiple media, active learning based on "collectively seeking, sieving, and synthesizing experiences", expression through non-linear associational webs of representations, and co-design by teachers and students of personalized learning experiences. title: Newton's Playground: a 2D drawing-based game for qualitative physics
description: Newton's Playground (NP) is a 2D video game aimed at helping middle school students understand qualitative physics, a nonverbal understanding of Newton's three laws, balance, mass, gravity, and energy. It is "a nonlinear video game (i.e. , a game design feature that allows many possible solution paths) where players are challenged to guide a green ball to a red balloon in a 2D environment." Players draw simple machines (ramps, levers, pendulums, springboards) that come to life and obey gravity and Newton's laws. The game contains 74 puzzles across 7 progressively more difficult playgrounds, with silver and gold trophies marking progress.

description: The authors recommend that neuropsychological training be included as a component of comprehensive intervention strategies for individuals with childhood trauma. They argue that "Neuropsychological training should be implemented in a comprehensive intervention strategy for individuals with childhood trauma" and that early intervention may prevent long-term deficits in memory function and academic performance in maltreated children.

article_title: Adolescents and adults need inhibitory control to compare fractions
citation: Rossi, S., Vidal, J., Letang, M., Houdé, O., & Borst, G. (2019). Adolescents and Adults Need Inhibitory Control to Compare Fractions. Journal of Numerical Cognition, 5(3), 314-336. https://doi.org/10.5964/jnc.v5i3.197
title: The negative priming paradigm adapted to misleading strategies as a tool for revealing inhibitory control in school learning
description: The negative priming paradigm, originally designed by Tipper (1985), rests on the logic that "if a distractor (or a strategy) is inhibited on a given item (i.e., the prime), then its activation on the following item (i.e., the probe) should be disrupted". The authors adapted this paradigm so that the misleading strategy required on the prime becomes appropriate on the probe, allowing them to test whether inhibiting the 'greater the whole number, the greater the fraction' strategy is needed to compare fractions with common numerators. The paradigm has been applied across school-learning domains including literacy, mathematics and science to reveal the inhibition of overlearned misleading heuristics.
requirements: Participants must succeed above chance level on the control and test primes for priming effects on the probes to be observed
constraints: The paradigm reveals that a misleading heuristic must be inhibited but provides no information on the strategy that is activated once the misleading heuristic has been inhibited
target_learners: adolescents (Grade 9)
educated adults (undergraduates)
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude comparison
overcoming the natural number bias
examples: In the test trials, participants compared common-numerator fractions on the prime (requiring inhibition of the misleading strategy) and then common-denominator fractions on the probe, where the strategy was appropriate.

article_title: Emerging Support for a Role of Exercise in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Intervention Planning
citation: Berwid Olga G., Halperin Jeffrey M. (2012). Emerging Support for a Role of Exercise in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Intervention Planning. Current Psychiatry Reports. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11920-012-0297-4
title: Neurodevelopmental compensation account: ADHD symptom remission reflects later-developing cortical circuitry compensating for underlying deficits via top-down regulatory control
description: The review proposes that ADHD arises from delayed cortical development — children with ADHD follow a trajectory of cortical maturation "delayed by 2 – 3 years relative to their typically-developing peers" — and that symptom decline with age reflects the degree to which later-developing higher cortical circuitry compensates through top-down regulatory control. On this account, remitting individuals show relative normalization of executive functioning and underlying circuitry. The authors use this framework to argue for interventions that enhance neural growth in executive-functioning brain regions.
requirements: Interventions on this account must target underlying neural mechanisms of ADHD rather than symptoms alone
constraints: The authors note normalization of the developmental trajectory being linked to improved outcomes is emerging, not established, data
target_learners: children with ADHD
target_learning_goals: executive functioning and cognitive control development
examples: The review cites longitudinal neuroimaging showing delayed cortical maturation in ADHD and relative normalization of executive functioning in remitters versus persisters

article_title: Neural changes underlying the development of episodic memory during middle childhood
citation: Ghetti Simona; Bunge Silvia A. (2012). Neural Changes Underlying the Development of Episodic Memory During Middle Childhood. Developmental cognitive neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2012.05.002
title: Network account of episodic memory development: concerted maturation of hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and parietal cortex plus long-range connectivity
description: The review's central explanatory framework holds that episodic memory development emerges from a distributed brain network rather than a single region. It proposes that "changes in episodic memory emerge from the concerted effort of a network of relevant brain structures," including local maturational changes in the hippocampus, lateral PFC, and posterior parietal cortex, and changes in long-range connectivity via the uncinate fasciculus, cingulum bundle, and fornix. Hippocampal binding is argued to continue developing during middle childhood rather than being age-invariant, alongside PFC-mediated controlled encoding and retrieval processes.
requirements: Structural or functional neuroimaging evidence tracking multiple network regions and their connecting tracts across development
constraints: An assessment of the relationship between the development of the network as a whole and behavioral changes has yet to be undertaken, per the article's conclusion
target_learners: typically developing children in middle childhood (roughly ages 6–11)
target_learning_goals: episodic memory: encoding, storage, and retrieval of events with contextual detail
examples: The review integrates longitudinal MRI, cross-sectional fMRI, and DTI findings across studies to argue for coordinated hippocampal, prefrontal, and parietal development.

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: Nelson and Narens' two-level metacognition model applied to regulation of divergent thinking
description: The article applies Nelson and Narens' (1990) model of metamemory to divergent thinking in creative processes. The model posits two levels—an object-level running executive processes (task performance, learning processes) and a meta-level holding a dynamic representation of the object-level—connected by two types of information flow: monitoring (from object-level to meta-level) and control (from meta-level to object-level). The authors use this framework to explain how "regulation of executive processes is enhanced" through a cyclic flow between levels, grounding their instructional design for metacognitive strategy instruction in divergent thinking.
requirements: Learners must possess metacognitive knowledge about tasks, strategies and self to assess task demands and outcomes
Strategy knowledge about the specific executive process (here, divergent thinking) is needed for accurate control
constraints: Applied in the article specifically to divergent thinking processes in visual arts education
target_learners: Secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Monitor and control divergent thinking processes to generate more original ideas
examples: In the intervention lesson, monitoring was enhanced through clarifying knowledge and misunderstandings about creativity, while control was stimulated through interactive discussion providing examples of strategy selection and implementation

citation: Ballard, H. L. (2023). Community and citizen science in schools: nested inquiries, productive tensions, and the role of communities. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09643-7

nature of science and uncertainty
using science for decision-making and action
identity and agency development

Autonomy support included meaningful rationales, acknowledging negative feelings, inviting language and self-pacing; competence support included structure, informational positive feedback, progress indication and criteria-based evaluation; relatedness support included researcher-mentor messages, forum sharing and a personal welcome (Tables 1-2).

article_title: ICT-support for grounding in the classroom
citation: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5
title: Negotiation of common ground as a dual concept combining linguistic and cognitive approaches
description: The article combines the linguistic approach of Clark and Schaefer with the cognitivist approach of Bromme into one account of grounding. In this conceptualisation, "negotiation of common ground is conceived of as a dual concept": negotiation of meaning, in which unshared understanding is made public, verified, clarified and re-verified until the grounding criterion is met, and negotiation of position, in which members make their private opinions public and check they are understood. Grounding starts when team members contribute unshared knowledge, and representational differences are minimised iteratively through feedback based on one's own perspective. This framework is the design basis for the NTool formalism.

constraints: The article's formalism is prescriptive and task-oriented, facilitating grounding related to the task at hand and disregarding other grounding activities, theoretically departing from Clark and Schaefer and Bromme

citation: Kullberg, N., Kiili, C., Bråten, I., González-Ibáñez, R., & Leppänen, P. H. T. (2023). Sixth graders' selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09613-5
title: Neurone web-based platform with snippet selection and writing tools for online inquiry

The snippet tool let students highlight and save up to two snippets per text (maximum 20 words each); the writing tool displayed selected snippets beside the writing space and let students open the source page with snippets highlighted in context. Copy-paste from snippets was blocked, and both tools were designed to save cognitive resources for integration.

citation: Double, K. S., & Birney, D. P. (2018). Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task. Metacognition and Learning, 13, 309–326. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-018-9186-5

description: The article adopts the Nelson and Narens framework to conceptualise how metacognitive consequences give rise to differential reactivity effects. The framework "distinguishes between an object-level where cognitive activity occurs, and a meta-level that governs the object-level processes", linked by upward monitoring and downward control processes. The authors operationalize monitoring as retrospective appraisals of performance and control as response-time behaviour, using the framework to generate hypotheses about how CR affect each pathway.

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review
citation: Sonja Dieterich, Stefan Rumann, Marc Rodemer. (2025). Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10071-x
title: Theory of negative knowledge as the review's conceptual framework for learning from errors
description: The review adopts the theory of negative knowledge by Oser et al. (1999, 2012) as its conceptual framework because it directly addresses how learning is supported by engaging with errors. According to the review, "encountering errors fosters negative knowledge, i.e., an understanding of what is wrong, which complements positive knowledge, i.e., how to do something correctly". The theory attributes a preventive function to negative knowledge: recognizing incorrect procedures helps reinforce correct approaches and avoid future mistakes without personally making the errors. Several included studies drew on this theory to explain their results.
requirements: Errors must be intentionally embedded in instructional materials for learners to retrace and often correct
constraints: The review notes cascade theory focuses on learners' own errors, whereas this framework addresses errors of others embedded in instruction

university students in the first to sixth semesters
vocational education and training students
target_learning_goals: negative knowledge about what is wrong
positive knowledge of correct principles and procedures
examples: Several studies included in this review draw on the theory of negative knowledge to explain their results on (contrasting) erroneous examples, including Barbieri et al. (2021), Heemsoth and Heinze (2014), Loibl and Leuders (2018), and Wernecke et al. (2018)

citation: Allen, KA., Gray, D.L., Baumeister, R.F., & Leary, M.R. (2022). The Need to Belong: a Deep Dive into the Origins, Implications, and Future of a Foundational Construct. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 1133–1156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09633-6
title: The need to belong: desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation
description: The need-to-belong construct, originating in Baumeister and Leary's influential 1995 paper titled "The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation," posits that the desire for interpersonal attachments is a fundamental human motivation. The article revisits this foundational construct through an interview with its originators to "explore the value and relevance of belonging for understanding human behavior and promoting well-being." It serves as the explanatory framework underpinning the article's review of belonging research in educational psychology.

title: Nelson and Narens' metamemory model as a normative framework for designing monitoring accuracy interventions
description: The article uses Nelson and Narens' (1990) metamemory model, which distinguishes an object level of cognitive processes and a meta level of metacognitive judgment, with monitoring informing the meta level and judgments driving control decisions. The meta-analysis concludes that "Monitoring accuracy can thus be improved by providing support on each component of Nelson and Narens' (1990) metamememory model," suggesting the descriptive model can serve as a normative framework for developing successful instructional interventions.

target_learning_goals: Accurate metacognitive monitoring of problem-solving performance

article_title: Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories
citation: Lisette Hornstra, Kim Stroet, Christine Rubie-Davies, Annaline Flint. (2023). Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09788-4
title: Need-supportive teaching in SDT: three dimensions (autonomy support, structure, involvement) and their thwarting counterparts
description: Within SDT's Basic Psychological Needs Theory, educational literature identifies "three dimensions of need-supportive teaching" that support students' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Autonomy support includes offering choices, fostering relevance, and cognitive autonomy support via open questions. Structure provides contingent information, guidance, optimal challenge, clear guidelines, and non-comparative feedback. Involvement shows unconditional positive regard and commitment to students' learning. Need support and need thwarting are "two independent dimensions": controlling teaching, chaos, and disaffection actively threaten needs and can cause need frustration and outcomes such as amotivation or dropout.
requirements: Need support should be tailored to the individual student and contingent on students' needs, abilities, and actions, rather than applied as a one-size-fits-all approach
constraints: SDT research has focused mostly on between-teacher differences in need support, with little attention to ability grouping or within-teacher variation
target_learners: school students
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation
engagement
well-being
need satisfaction
examples: In a multiple case study the review cites, socio-constructivist schools provided autonomy support via scaffolding in one-on-one interactions, while a traditional school used open, cognitively engaging questions in whole-class instruction

citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Nepantla and world-traveling: multiple selves at the margins of social worlds
description: Drawing on Anzaldúa and Lugones, the article theorizes that individuals hold multiple selves that move across social worlds, and that marginalized people must 'travel' between worlds as a matter of necessity and survival. Nepantla is 'an in-between liminal state of being that is the result of world traveling,' a painful but potentially transformative space where clashing worldviews collide. Moving through nepantla can liberate individuals from constraining norms and enable re-narration of limiting cultural scripts, linking psychological processes with structural realities.
requirements: Transformation requires moving through the discomfort of nepantla rather than retreating from it, which Anzaldúa argues thwarts its transformative potential
constraints: The account is theoretical and draws on scholars theorizing life at the margins of multiple social worlds; it is not an empirically tested model in this article
target_learners: marginalized undergraduate students navigating multiple cultural worlds
target_learning_goals: sustaining authentic plural selves while succeeding in dominant institutional settings
examples: Valle and Covarrubias (2024) documented five low-income, first-generation Mexican American women resisting racist, sexist, and classist scripts and creating new narratives; Bernal (2001) explored Chicana undergraduates leveraging plurality to navigate college challenges

citation: Psyridou, M., Koponen, T., Tolvanen, A., Aunola, K., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Torppa, M. (2024). Early prediction of math difficulties with the use of a neural networks model. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(2), 212-232. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000835
title: Neural networks (multilayer perceptron) models as a prediction-oriented approach to early identification of learning difficulties
description: The article frames deep neural networks as machine-learning models that, unlike classical linear, inference-focused statistics, can identify linear and non-linear associations, interaction effects, or combinations of these, and can handle many correlated predictors. A multilayer perceptron learns connection weights from labelled training data and is then applied to a held-out testing sample to forecast a dichotomized outcome. The authors position this as a complement to inference models: "Prediction allows, for example, the identification of whether an individual will experience MD without requiring an understanding of the underlying mechanisms". They also name the approach's key limitation: neural networks are often referred to as black boxes.

target_learning_goals: early identification of children at risk of math difficulties (arithmetic fluency)

citation: T. P. Reber and N. Rothen (2018). Educational App-Development needs to be informed by the Cognitive Neurosciences of Learning & Memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0039-4
title: Memory-related educational apps should be developed on the basis of fundamental principles from the cognitive neuroscience of memory, with theoretically motivated features varied within the app for large-scale long-term testing
description: The article proposes that educational ICT, especially memory-related apps such as foreign-language learning apps, "need to be developed on the basis of fundamental principles derived from cognitive neuroscience of memory". college students

target_learning_goals: memory-based learning such as vocabulary acquisition
skill and knowledge outcomes measured by school grades

In this study a fully open-source pipeline deployed MXBAI embeddings and LLaMa 2 70B on a corpus of "125 VNS-related peer-reviewed publications and technical documentation" curated by three faculty members through independent selection, consensus review, and validation that the corpus contained all information needed to answer every MCQ question.
requirements: The corpus must be curated and verified to contain all information necessary to answer the target questions, as the faculty did for the 125-publication VNS corpus
constraints: Corpus curation inevitably introduces selective biases that influence information quality, comprehensiveness, and currency, per the article's technical considerations section
target_learners: practicing neurosurgeons performing VNS procedures
target_learning_goals: VNS-related clinical management, surgical anatomy, procedural steps, and technical aspects for drug-resistant epilepsy
examples: The system was benchmarked against 36 masterclass-trained neurosurgeons on a 14-item MCQ, scoring 0.75 versus a best individual score of 0.68

description: The National Educational Panel Study Starting Cohort 2 (Kindergarten, SC2) is a nationwide German longitudinal panel; the authors used it because it "comprised information on developing competencies from kindergarten to the different secondary school levels". title: Assign a unique set of raters to each student within a nested r:(p×i) design to enhance reliability and reduce assessment time under resource constraints
description: The article proposes that when time or raters are scarce, SBL assessments should use a nested design in which "subsets of raters evaluate different students, rather than each rater assessing every student", which "can reduce potential rater fatigue and inconsistencies". In the course's nested r:(p×i) structure, two raters with ten items reached a Phi-coefficient of 0.83, whereas the crossed design required three raters. The authors state a nested design "should be considered when time or resource constraints are present".

citation: Zhang Huiqun, Li Shanshan, Zheng Guoquan, Chen Xiaoyun, Zhong Lujie, Li Jiaying, Li Yun. (2025). Network analysis of an OSCE-based graduation skills assessment for clinical medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07091-0
title: Network analysis of OSCE modules as a lens on skill interdependence and centrality
description: The article applies psychological-network methods to OSCE module scores, estimating a regularized partial correlation network (EBICglasso) and computing centrality indices, with expected influence treated as primary: "Expected influence (EI) is a measure calculated by adding up the weights of edges connected to a node in a network." High-EI nodes are read as modules whose improvement can boost related competencies, complementing t-tests, ANOVA, and correlations. Accuracy and stability were checked with bootnet bootstrapping, including correlation stability coefficients.
requirements: A sufficiently large sample for stable network estimation; the article reports CS coefficients should not fall below 0.25 and preferably exceed 0.5
constraints: The authors state the methodology "may not fully capture the complexity of clinical skill interdependencies"
target_learners: undergraduate clinical medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical skills competence as measured by OSCE graduation assessment
examples: The article estimated two networks over 11 OSCE items, found 44 of 55 edges non-zero, and validated stability with 1,000 bootstrap iterations

title: Near-peer teaching in surgery rests on social constructivism, building knowledge through social interaction between trainees of similar experience
description: The article frames trainee-as-trainer as near-peer teaching, an instructional approach in which more junior learners are taught by slightly more senior trainees in the workplace. The authors ground it theoretically: "It is based upon social constructivism, where knowledge is built through social interactions in the learning environment." They cite evidence that near-peer teaching can enhance trainees' self-efficacy and improve job satisfaction, while noting barriers such as perceptions that teaching is burdensome or insecurity about teaching someone of similar experience level.
requirements: Willingness of the senior trainee to let the junior operate, and balancing supervision with independence, cited as attributes of a successful surgical trainer

target_learning_goals: Operative skills through near-peer intraoperative teaching
Trainee self-efficacy and teaching capability
examples: A trainee-as-trainer case in which a Junior Registrar performed the appendicectomy assisted by a Senior Registrar while a Core Trainee learned as assistant

title: Simulation modalities for neurosurgical technical skills training: synthetic manikins, locally developed synthetic models and porcine cadavers
description: The article describes an array of affordable, accessible training models and modalities available for neurosurgical training, including porcine cadavers, fresh frozen cadaveric tissue (significantly more expensive but high fidelity), synthetic manikins, and locally developed synthetic simulation models. Figure 1 shows a full body synthetic manikin for patient positioning and three-point rigid fixation with the Mayfield skull clamp, a silicone-moulded glass display head for flap design practice, and a synthetic model for EVD insertion with CSF drainage. Figure 2 shows pig cadaver use for spinal procedures such as pedicle screw insertion. The authors note ethical considerations including review board approval and laboratory protocols for biological models.
requirements: Ethical considerations must be observed for biological models, including obtaining review board approval and adhering to laboratory protocols
The primary focus should be on meeting learning objectives through effective SBE
constraints: Fresh frozen cadaveric tissue is significantly more expensive; pig cadavers lack realistic muscle groups and fascicle for anterior approaches and require bespoke licensed wet labs
target_learners: Neurosurgical trainees in early to mid-training
target_learning_goals: Practising prioritised procedural skills such as patient positioning, pinning, flap design, EVD insertion and spinal procedures before real patient encounters
examples: The article suggests a cost-effective synthetic-based manikin for patient positioning and pinning practice, anonymized MRI or CT images from real patients to support flap design discussion, and notes a single simulation model may accommodate practice of both EVD insertion and ICP probe insertion via Kocher's point

description: The article invokes the neurovisceral integration model proposed by Thayer and colleagues to explain why HRV metrics track expertise during simulated procedures. constraints: The article notes the simulation involved neither real patients nor real radiation, so workload levels might have been considerably lower than under real-life circumstances

article_title: Social withdrawal and academic achievement, intertwined over years? Bidirectional effects from primary to upper secondary school.
citation: Stenseng, F., Tingstad, E. B., Wichstrøm, L., & Skalicka, V. (2022). Social withdrawal and academic achievement, intertwined over years? Bidirectional effects from primary to upper secondary school. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 92, 1354–1365. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12504
title: Need-to-belong account of the withdrawal–achievement interplay
description: The article interprets its gendered bidirectional findings through need-to-belong theory, in which humans have "a fundamental motivation to create and maintain long-term relationships". When belongingness is thwarted, a stressful state emerges that burdens cognitive and regulatory resources, impairing attention and persistence needed for learning. Conversely, higher achievement may raise self-esteem and peer status, making withdrawn children more attractive as learning partners and reducing withdrawal, producing cascade-like reciprocal effects.
requirements: Applies to social withdrawal rooted in conflicted shyness, where the child is socially motivated but fails to participate, rather than to volitional solitude
constraints: The article notes the study assessed only the conflicted shyness dimension of the Child Social Preference Scale, leaving out social disinterest and active isolation, which may relate differently to achievement
target_learners: schoolchildren from primary to upper secondary school (ages 6–14)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading, writing and mathematics
social functioning and classroom participation
examples: The authors propose a positive cycle in which increased achievement boosts self-esteem, social status and motivation for peer interaction, which reduces shyness and improves self-regulation and learning skills

description: The study structured its needs analysis around Hoadley-Maidment's needs analysis triangle, which distinguishes student-perceived, teacher-perceived and company-perceived needs, alongside Golden and McGaghie's argument that healthcare education design must link to healthcare needs. constraints: The balance of rigour and feasibility meant only two clinical specialties were represented in the expert clinician group

target_learning_goals: identifying and prioritising learning needs for simulation-based education

description: The article reviews mechanistic accounts of mental imagery, contrasting a controversial neuromuscular theory (fine peripheral muscle activity during imagery, with conflicting EMG evidence) with a cognitive theory holding that MI facilitates central coding and strengthens cognitive representations. It states that functional MRI and PET studies "showed that there are an activation of similar brain areas during an imagined movement compared to physically performed movement", supporting a "neurofunctional equivalence" between imagined and executed movement, alongside an isochrony principle of similar movement durations.

constraints: The neuromuscular theory is described as controversial, with EMG findings both supporting (Guillot et al.) and opposing (Gentilli et al.) it
target_learners: Learners acquiring technical or gestural skills
target_learning_goals: Understanding how mental rehearsal supports motor skill acquisition
examples: The article cites Jacobson's 1931 observation of fine peripheral muscle activity during imagery as the origin of the neuromuscular account.

title: Neurophysiological and psychosocial perspectives on how physical activity benefits cognition and academic achievement
description: The article presents two non-exclusive explanatory accounts for the PA–achievement link. The neurophysiological perspective holds that PA offers direct positive effects on the brain, increasing blood flow, metabolism and growth factors such as BDNF, improving memory, attention and learning. The psychosocial perspective holds that PA with peers improves social skills, self-esteem and emotional wellbeing, indirectly supporting achievement. The article states these explanations "are not exclusionary" and that understanding of the relationship is still in an initial phase.
requirements: Both perspectives are offered as explanations requiring further research; the article states many issues remain to be clarified
constraints: The article states the mechanisms by which PA may offer benefits to AA are not well-known

title: NEPS framework of three dimensions of instructional quality applied to private tutoring
description: The NEPS framework for out-of-school learning environments characterizes the instructional quality of private tutoring in the same manner as classroom lessons. As the article states, "It differentiates between the dimensions of structure, challenge, and support in private tutoring and is closely related to the framework of three basic dimensions of teaching quality". Challenge means cognitive activation of learners, support refers to the teacher–student relationship including feedback and handling of errors, and structure comprises well-structured content presentation and effective time management. The study empirically confirmed this three-factor structure for tutoring via confirmatory factor analyses.
requirements: Student ratings of tutoring on the 11 NEPS items covering structure, challenge, and support
constraints: The article notes connections to research on one-to-one instruction, such as tutor–student dialogue quality, are missing and should be integrated into the challenge dimension in future research
target_learners: secondary school students receiving private tutoring
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in mathematics, German, and English
student well-being and satisfaction with school and family situation
examples: The framework was operationalized with 11 four-point items in NEPS Wave 3 and evaluated with confirmatory factor analyses in three subjects

citation: Harveson Andrew T., Hannon James C., Brusseau Timothy A., Podlog Leslie, Papadopoulos Charilaos, Hall Morgan S., Celeste EvaRose. (2019). title: Neurotrophic stimulation hypothesis as the authors' preferred mechanism for resistance exercise's cognitive benefits
description: The article invokes the neurotrophic stimulation hypothesis, which "states that neuromuscular activity stimulates areas of the brain that control executive function, resource allocation, and speed of processing." The authors believe it "is most applicable to our findings," reasoning that neuromuscular adaptations from resistance exercise explain why it improved academic achievement and cognition over aerobic exercise and control. They also cite resistance exercise's demonstrated ability to increase brain-derived neurotrophic factor and the greater task complexity of resistance exercise as complementary accounts.
requirements: The hypothesis is offered as an interpretation of the study's findings, not as a mechanism tested within the study itself.
constraints: The article states additional research should isolate the precise mechanisms driving improvements in executive function; the cerebral blood flow hypothesis would predict similar benefits for both modalities, which was not observed.
target_learners: middle school students (eighth grade)
target_learning_goals: executive function and selective attention
academic achievement in mathematics
examples: The authors contrast the neurotrophic account with the cerebral blood flow hypothesis, which should theoretically have enhanced performance similarly after both moderate-intensity exercise modalities.
